britannica-1911-macdonnell-alestair-ruad:
Alestair Ruadh Macdonnell, chief of Glengarry, is profiled in a 1911 Britannica article. He lived from about 1725 to 1761. He was a Scottish Jacobite. Andrew Lang identified him as the secret agent called Pickle. Pickle acted as a spy on Prince Charles Edward after 1750, the text says.

His family was a branch of the clan Macdonald. They spelt their name Macdonnell or Macdonell. His father was John, twelfth chief of Glengarry. He was a violent and brutal man, by the account. He is said to have starved his first wife to death. She was Alestair's mother, kept on an island in the Hebrides. Alestair ran away to France as a mere boy in 1738. There he entered the Royal Scots, a regiment in French service. In 1743 he commanded a company in it. In 1744 he was sent to Scotland as a Jacobite agent.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-dunchadh:
Dunchadh, abbot of Iona until his death in 717, ruled a famous monastery through years of disputed succession, and this entry maps the confusion. Son of Ceannfaeladh and grandson of Maelcobha, he first appears as abbot of Killochuir on the Ulster coast. The annals then disagree over when he took Iona, with rival names and dates crowding the years 704 to 717. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 sets the rival claims side by side.

Part of the trouble was the paschal question, the old dispute over how to reckon Easter, which may have split the community. Dorbaine Foda and Faelchu both appear as abbots in those years, perhaps as coadjutors or priors under Dunchadh. The entry suits readers who want monastic politics in the raw, with dates argued rather than smoothed over.
